review: In short - Awesome, awesome, awesome remake to the awesome SH classing, and finally some breathe of life to the franchise.   ✅ Pros + Bloober Team respects original source material and enhances it greatly. + This has everything that made SH2 great and improving pretty much everything that can be improved without hurting the original magic: Better combat, better graphics, better voice acting, awesome soundtrack + Great scared, eerie tone and psychological fear + Can easily be a strong entry point for newbies to Silent Hill or survival horror games. + Difficulty feels fair and balanced while still challenging, on Normal (Action\Puzzles) + There's puzzles difficultly and combat difficulty, yay!  ⚖️ If that's your thing: +/- Classic Survival Horror games can at many times feel like closed doors simulator, and the remake doesn't so anything to change this (Which I personally didn't expect or mind) +/- Combat is greatly improved but still feels clunky, in a genre-fitting way I believe +/- Linear and relatively short (As pretty much most SH games)  ❌ Cons None!   Longer version no one reads:  I'm finishing this game with a sigh of relief, as looks like at least for the time being, Silent Hill is back on track.  After having played and loved almost all main Silent Hill games (Besides Downpour, on which I didn't get my hands on yet) (And yeah, I loved even Homecoming!), Seemed Silent Hill went dead forever, and then we got.... Well, Silent Hill Ascension, which was.... Ugh, let's not get into it. But then we got THIS.  I was expecting the remake for a long time, and having also played and enjoyed The Medium by Bloober I also had faith they'd do a good job, but still had doubts as their previous games weren't so much action oriented.  I guess making a remake is somewhat easier in that case as they didn't have to create something completely anew but more of re-doing some already existing powerful source material. While I'm not that hardcore fan which completed every SH 20 times - I've only completed the original once, and that was many years ago, so I cannot point out all the differences etc. Still in my honest opinion, I feel Bloober did a perfect job in this one - much respect to the source material, they're really managed to capture the magic and horror of the original game, preserving what worked and improving everything that could be improved - The soundtrack remains loyal to the original with some musical overhaul from time to time (which I liked). The new voice overs work well and capture the eeriness and weirdness of the original characters. Graphics are obviously overhauled and look modern and pretty darn good (and scary!). Script and story remained mostly (if not completely) the same as far as I can remember, which is a good thing. Combat is greatly improved and feels mostly great, while still keeping that survival-horror awkwardness (which some may feel is a "bug" and some a "feature", but I think it serves the game just right). I think some puzzles were replaced but I've enjoyed the whole experienced on Normal from beginning to an end. Quality of scares does not fall short from original game and there's just the right balance between jump scares and some freaking psychological fear (Oh and that damn limbs monster got me squeaking every time!)  I feel this game can also serve as a great entry point for newcomers to both Silent Hill and\or Survival Horror, this is truly a modern version capturing all the best things about Silent Hill, in my opinion. I can see why some might prefer a more Resident-Evil-ish direction when SH games can sometimes feel like closed doors simulator, but hey, isn't that part of Survival Horroring?  Already expecting to play Silent Hill F although not by same dev, but seems it's doing pretty well by the reviews, and mainly I'm very happy having some attention and actual resources going towards this series, and very hopeful we'll keep seeing some more quality stuff from the franchise (And I wouldn't mind another remake as well (=;  )

review: I wanted to like this game, unfortunately I don't. This is not Silent Hill 2. This is not Psychological Horror. The heavy focus on combat and the ridiculous number of overly aggressive enemies destroy the pace and atmosphere of the game. I lowered the action level in hopes that it would make the gameplay more tolerable but it had no impact that I could detect. I understand how the combat system works, its not complex, in fact it has no variety at all which makes it tedious and monotonous. Dodge, attack, dodge, attack, repeat endlessly on the hordes of enemies everywhere.   I admit the combat in the original is also clunky and not fun, but that game doesn't constantly swarm James with hyper-aggressive hoards of enemies to force the issue. Combat always felt optional, it was an afterthought and not the point of the experience. In the remake the combat is the entire point and is required to be able to enjoy exploration due to the highly aggressive design of the enemies.  The environments in this game are also unnecessarily bloated, which also destroys the pace and atmosphere. Combined with the overly numerous and aggressive enemies in every single room and hall it creates a feeling that nothing of substance is ever happening as well as creating a disassociation with the story and characters. The reality is that Silent Hill 2 doesn't have a long story, it doesn't take long to tell, 5-6 hours is all you need. Why is every environment in this remake 3 times longer than it needs to be? The Woodside apartments were so overextended and bloated that I almost quit when I reached the Blue Creek Apartments because I was so tired of the apartments and the constant combat. I am now 7 hours in and just completed the Blue Creek Apartments and honestly, I don't want to play anymore. I don't know if I will ever finish this game. This just isn't fun, its a slog.  I don't know how much of the blame falls on Bloober Team and how much falls on Konami but I suspect Konami bares the lions share of blame.

review: The original Silent Hill 2 is a prisonic fairytale of historic proportions. This reimagining doubles down on all the macabre, filthy, nerve racking, delightfully miserable and downright excruciating aspects of the iconic survival horror experience. The original is still a superior and more concise piece of art that deserves endless praise for its genius game designs, but the effort from Bloober team is exceptionally faithful to the source, while offering long time fans of Silent Hill and all newcomers a deeper dive into the depths of the abyss than the original game offered. The game is more than twice the runtime of the original with brand new level designs and segments. The combat system is very simple, but proactive and fun, which keeps the exploration loop flowing. The boss fights in this game are probably the best in the entire series. If you love survival horror, then play this game.   It's a nearly 10/10 with a few simple mods like increasing your movement speed, increasing the camera distance, and removing the weapon sway. Play the game without any hints or prompts on Hard mode. Tune your HDR settings right as well to get the best black level. Performance of UE5 is hit or miss, just don't use raytracing.

review: Easily one of the best horror games I've played in a while. The pace, the game loop, graphics, sound, story and environments. It's the right amount of scary without being stressful. Not too forgiving with resources, yet generous enough. Puzzles are fun. Fighting mechanics are intuitive.  I've been a fan of horror games since the first Resident Evil came out. But for some reason I just could not get into Silent Hill, despite being such a popular franchise. And it was not because I didn't want it, but because circumstances never let it happen.  It was until the PS3 era when I first got to play one: Silent Hill Homecoming. While that game is universally hated, it was my first Silent Hill and I found it to be an amazing horror game. The only negatives I could find was the bad controls and overall performance, which was not very good.  I don't feel that this game is that different in terms of content, but just the fact that it is very well polished and the graphics have been improved, make it a much more enjoyable experience.  I don't have much to say in terms of lore and such because this is my second Silent Hill, and my first mainline title. Compared to the only Silent Hill I've played before, it feels like it follows the same formula (I know I'll get destroyed by SH fans for saying this).  I never expected to enjoy it as much as I have. I don't think I can find any negatives about this game. Even performance has been solid. No crashes, stuttering, FPS dips, etc. Maxed out graphics, 1440p, RT on, 120fps. And it plays great with a generic Xbox One controller.

review: Genuinely the best survival horror game in since probably re7 imo. The game is gorgeous with RT on and the sound design might be the best in a horror game i've played. Be warned, its not a "fun" story nor is it really a fun game to play.   Its not a jump scare heavy type of game in the vein of visage or similar but instead it simply uses dread & suspense that doesnt go away, from the apartment section to the hospital(and beyond) it simply never really gives you a time to breath.  The combat is mostly ok with a similar feeling to RE2 remake but just alot slower in general, James isnt really the quickest character to move around or hit things with. There's not alot of enemy variation either but i think its more ok than usual since combat isnt constant(maybe except for the prison area) and while i enjoyed the combat it does drag on a bit towards the end. Healing items & ammunition might be given a bit to often tbh, i think i had around 30 heals throughout the last areas to the end of the game which made some areas & bosses very trivial and easy to fight through.  I think James is my favourite game protagonist in a long time, he is not perfect in the slightest but you cant help but you cant help but to feel sorry for the dude, he is just depressed as hell and is not having a good time throughout the game.   The only real downside is the length, i finished the game in about 14.5 hours which could have and should have been cut down a few hours(specially parts of the hospital & the labyrinth). Those areas that drag on are not bad at all but just feels a bit boring to go  through after a while(thinking of the otherworld hospital here etc).  Its a 9/10 for me and a actual must play for most people, even tho its a scary game i think the story and its themes are things people very much should experience and also talk about.

review: While Bloober Team did a thoroughly commendable job in handling the assignment that they were given and surpassed the expectations of naysayers and doubters, and the actors in this game all did a great job at translating the performances of the original into a more modern, "earnest" delivery, there are many tonal, writing, and directing issues that persist and ultimately detract from what was once a masterfully-designed narrative. I am interested to see the SH1 remake and think there's a lot of opportunity for Bloober to not only recapture the essence of the original while also improving upon it, but for those that have never played the original Silent Hill 2 for the PS2/XBOX, this is an artistic downgrade from the original. I'm going to try to organize my issues into an internet-friendly numbered list.  1.) Tone: While much of the game is decidedly as dour and depressing as the original was, it lacks the feelings of desperation, confusion, surrealism and general illness the original had. This is seen most frequently in the reworked soundtrack from legendary series musical composer Akira Yamaoka, who collaborated with other musicians in "updating" the original soundtrack. While the songs are nice new renditions in and of themselves the choice of genre often distracts from the tone that original scenes were attempting to establish. Case in point, the scene where [spoiler]James first meets Maria on the docks. Not only does the remake place heavy iconographic focus on this moment by making the spot where you first meet Maria a gazebo distanced far out from the docks rather than just on a stroll across them, but the tone of the music is more sensual than the original in a way I feel is actually completely emotionally inappropriate for what James is actually feeling in that moment. In the original, when Null Moon plays, the tone is a lot more somber and paints a picture of confusion that James is experiencing upon seeing a woman that looks nearly identical to his dead wife, who's flirting with him. It feels totally wrong to James, and the player, in that moment.[/spoiler] There are other instances of the tone and music not quite matching up with the emotionality of the original, but that's probably the most glaring example.  2.) Writing: There are many shortcomings that the game face in its writing of new character dialogue and endings. I'm going to pick on Eddie here when discussing the characters (and we'll get back to him later, too). [spoiler]Eddie now asks James if he can come with him from the Blue Creek Apartments building when they first meet, to which James rejects. This is a departure from the original in such a way that I feel misses the point and intentions behind Eddie's character relative to James as someone who lacks the self-awareness to confront his guilt over his evil deeds, and instead positions him as a generic "survivor in a dilapidated town" one might expect from a Resident Evil game upon first meeting him. In the original, he's just throwing up in a toilet and doesn't request to come with James. It's a bizarre scene meant to give the player unease, not relief that another person is near.[/spoiler] As for the new endings, [spoiler]Bliss[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Stillness[/spoiler], they somewhat miss the point of the original's default and NG+ Rebirth endings. [spoiler]Bliss transports James inside the videotape of Mary at Lakeview Hotel, and under a charitable interpretation has him do this under the pretense that he doesn't want to confront his guilt or trauma and will continue living the memory of Mary prior to her death rather than come to terms with what he did. Functionally, on a literal narrative level this ending basically makes James' journey null and void without having the emotional maturity of the default original endings. On a psychological level it's pretty much identical to Rebirth, just lacking the emotional punch. Stillness opts instead to expand upon the In Water ending in a frankly somewhat corny and uninteresting way by having a manifestation of Mary show up in James' car seat, alive and telling him to join her. Blugh.[/spoiler] To prove that I'm not just being a negative nancy or an anti-Bloober sycophant, there are some positives to the writing additions made by Bloober, all centering around the most surprising character: Angela. Upon this game's announcement Angela's character was the one fans feared receiving the worst remake treatment, as Bloober hasn't shown the most sensitivity surrounding the sensitive subject matter that Angela's character was meant to address, but the new scene she's given (while still only reiterating what we already knew about her) is good and keeps her at the forefront of the player's mind. There are also additional memos to read that subtly reinforce the main themes of the game appropriately, but overall the concision of the original is left in favor of bloat.  3.) Direction: This is the big one. Part of this is addressed in Tone with the musical direction but there are so many little things about the specific [b]direction[/b] of the performances. Overall I had very little issue with the actors and feel like they did a fine job with what they were given, but the fundamental Lynchian direction of the original is basically vacuum-sealed out of this thing. To pick on Eddie again, [spoiler]the scene where he confronts James in the meat locker and begins crashing out over the bullying he received over the course of the years leading up to his crimes. For some reason the voice director and the writer in charge of adapting the script told the voice actor to read out the line "You fat disgusting piece of..." and all that follows without any quotation marks. In the original game, he's recounting what other people said about him and the performance reflects that. In the remake, the lack of direction indicating quotation means that Eddie's just saying this to James without any context in a really confusing and dumb way.[/spoiler] Almost an hour and a half later, once Eddie is no longer in the plot, there is a scene [spoiler]in the Otherworld version of Lakeview Hospital you come across a voice recording device used by a doctor, which is supposed to be the doctor that was treating Mary's illness. In the original, upon interacting with this, the camera pans out to a bed floating in the air, and the player is forced to listen to his words while the surreal image of the fog wafting around the bed over the view of the water plays out. In the remake, it's no different than activating a BioShock audio log. No surrealist imagery, no forceful reckoning with the truth- in fact, you can leave the room entirely and not have the log continue playing, which defeats the purpose and emotional weight found in the original.[/spoiler] But then, the part that really made me scratch my head the most and realize the ultimate problem with this game was the reading of Mary's letter. For all my complaints about performance thus far I want to make it abundantly clear that Mary/Maria's remake VA is not at fault for any of the issues I have with it- the original was literally lightning in a bottle that couldn't be recaptured. In the original game's voice recording sessions, the actress, Monica Horgan, had not read the dialogue before recording. In a very emotionally-affecting moment, she begins to break down and cry while reading out the contents of the letter. Throughout the rest of the game we don't see characters undergo this kind of lucid mental and emotional catharsis, so for it to be placed at the very end feels like, regardless of which ending you get, a sobering and emotionally-resonant moment. In the remake the actress doesn't cry. Again, I don't blame her- the original performance was as iconic and emotional as it was by complete happenstance. Like the original game. This may be the only game I DON'T recommend that I'd give a 9/10 by itself. It's very good if you haven't played the original. Emulate the OG, tho.

review: Never ever have i played a better game in the horror genre than Silent Hill 2 (Remake). The psychological displeasure of this game is underlined with an atmosphere like no other. There are very few jumpscares, but the ones that actually are in the game are phenomenal. Because of this circumstance you always have to stay sharp and concentrated. But the true fact that makes this game so interesting is its unmatched ambient. Fog, noises, the people you meet, the town itself. You always ask yourself - "whats even happening here?" until the plot gets revealed and you do your own research afterwards, which is absolutely mindblowing once you realize the true nature of all the protagonists.  The little details are unmatched for this genre. Facial expressions, dialogue hints, metaphors - you name it. After finishing the game I was still very invested and to this day still I occasionally read lore or watch videos about the true meaning of many scenes, enemies, the main characters etc. even tho I finished the game nearly a year ago.  Combat is intense and very fair. It can feel slow at certain times, but thats exactly why fighting is so pleasurable. The remake is about twice as long as the original, which should already hint to you that the game is in many instances stale. Oftentimes I felt like they could have easily cut 20 minutes of gameplay from a certain level, and it wouldn't have affected the storyline adversely at all.  Some levels felt unnecessarily packed with monsters, so much that I felt like I was playing the Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. The riddles are another thing I want to critique. They oftentimes contain symbols that originate from medieval alchemy, which the average person obviously has never seen. The link to alchemy has some deeper meaning, but it isn't something that you would understand unless you genuinely were looking up what those symbols mean. The riddles are in many cases too simplistic and involve you having to find some pattern. The focus of the riddles almost always less grounded meaning, which is disappointing.  Finally, optimization is terrible. I have a decent PC, but mine struggled to run the game at 60 FPS most of the time. From what I read this seems to be a common issue among users. The game simply can't run smoothly unless you have an elite setup.

Floors lead to empty voids, interior ceilings may or may not exist, Silent Hill itself turns inside-out and adopts the appearance of machinery's interiors, and claustrophobia reigns supreme. Whether in the [spoiler]normal town[/spoiler] and its desolate, sinister, isolating aura, or the [spoiler]Otherworld[/spoiler] and its oppressive, screeching, decaying premise, the modern visuals never failed to disappoint.  At the same time, Silent Hill 2 is a captivating sight to behold: the story is utterly captivating and compelling, and seeing James Sunderland's slog through his rotting iron purgatory, replete with guilt, punishment, and cruel metaphors, will be hard for me to forget. From Half-Life 2 to Resident Evil 4 to Spec Ops: The Line, I've always loved the long, nearly-unbroken journey across a vast space, learning more about the characters as they overcome greater trials, and SH2 is no exception. Never played the original, so I can't say how accurate or faithful it is, but it doesn't really matter that much to me. The underlying themes of [spoiler]guilt, trauma, and active repression of memories over an atrocious but darkly-understandable action in the face of watching a loved one slowly die with no hope for a cure[/spoiler] is a series off raw gut-punches, wrought with disturbing visual metaphors in the environmental, enemy, and atmospheric design.  The realistic aspects of Silent Hill 2 were well-received; the voice acting and dialogue stayed perfectly believable, and the acting itself was excellent throughout. Every character was memorable: James and Pyramid Head for obvious reasons, but Maria's, Eddie's, and Laura's performances gave the game a perfectly surreal and unsettling atmosphere. Combat isn't particularly hard if you're good at resource management, but on the hardest difficulty, it's not easy either. Preserving bullets and medical supplies is crucial, but if you're diligent with melee, saving up a few dozen bullets or so is entirely doable. They'll be needed during boss fights. Puzzles aren't hard either, but if they're not your thing, the experience of walking back and forth between rooms to find trinkets for hours won't be overly fun. This game is a masterpiece to me, though, and a gold-standard remake of a classic psychological horror game that's guaranteed to stick around in a player's brain for years.

review: I've long wanted to play the remake of one of my favorite games. However, it so happened that I only just finished the entire playthrough - and coincidentally, I'm writing this review on its first anniversary.  Firstly, I still can't believe this game was actually released. I bought it as a way of thanking Team Silent for giving the world such a unique series of games (which, among other things, influenced me). Secondly, I realized I’d be getting a remake of the second installment as well.  It's important to note that, simply due to the unavailability of both retro consoles and original game discs, it would have been difficult for the average player to experience the originals. Now, a new generation of players unfamiliar with the series can explore a modernized version in a convenient format.  I didn't have the chance to try the original game with its authentic gameplay experience. For enthusiasts like me, the Enhanced Edition was created, immersing me in the world of Silent Hill - and with that experience in mind, I constantly compared it to the remake. And you know what? Bloober Team managed to capture almost the entirety of that same atmosphere. During my first playthrough, I couldn’t believe I was reliving the same familiar story. You experience the same emotions as before - from the ambient soundscape of the quiet town (thanks again to the incomparable Akira Yamaoka for the soundtrack) to the oppressive atmosphere of the otherworldly realm.  And indeed, knowing every plot twist didn’t make the game boring at all. On the contrary, the developers almost completely redesigned the levels, making the familiar story feel fresh again. This makes it more engaging even for seasoned players who know the original by heart. The story itself hasn’t undergone any major changes - which is good for both newcomers who want to explore this project and returning fans who simply want to immerse themselves in the same world once more.  One downside is that the game runs on Unreal Engine 5. While I’ll admit the graphics look incredible, the visuals were so demanding that the gameplay suffered from constant frame-rate drops and general instability (which was actually one of the reasons why it took me so long to complete the game). For those with slower PCs, I recommend launching the game with the parameter “-dx11.” Naturally, this disables many of the engine’s advanced features, but it ensures a much more stable experience - at least, that’s what worked for me. The choice of engine is a topic for debate, but this review isn’t about that. The most important thing is that I was able to fully enjoy the game.  In conclusion, the Silent Hill 2 Remake is exactly what it should be. It preserves the spirit and atmosphere of the original while adapting the gameplay to a modern over-the-shoulder format. This gives players a new sense of freedom when controlling James, along with redesigned level architecture and new puzzles. If the reader is faced with the choice of playing the remake instead of the original, I can only encourage that decision - because the developers have meticulously preserved the soul of the game while adapting it to modern standards.  Thank you for reading. Peace to all.

review: Wife guy horror game (defo not lots of those around).  In all seriousness, amazing game all around.  Level design: this is where the game shines and brings most of its elements together. If you haven't played a Silent Hill game, think of it like a Resident Evil game (closest comparable example I can think of is RE2R). It's a lot about exploring paths and solving puzzles, all while threading through perilous paths and challenging encounters (all heightened by the spooky aspect of the game). Enemy placements never feel unfair (aside from a few challenging encounters towards the end, but they're meant to be hard), but do require situational awareness. Puzzles (and level progress) is always rewarding (it's never too cut and clear but neither too hard, while still requiring some fair brain power for some).  Story and themes: a refined version of the original (imo), and the original is well remembered for a reason. I can't really go into the story itself, but if you haven't played it, there are 2 questions that you should keep in mind: "What is Silent Hill (and its purpose)?" and "Why are the present people here?". It explores deep themes of psychology, while making good use of presentation through gameplay more so than cinematics (which makes it paying attention all the more rewarding, but it isn't the level of interpretation from Soulsborne games if you're worried). There's also some subtle choices the game never makes you aware of that dictate the end of the game (an important aspect is related to a key game mechanic, but it's up to you to guess), instead of having the obvious "choose your ending" options (although if you really don't want to screw yourself over you can always save at the end of the game, as there will be a "choice" before your final confrontation).  Gameplay: as previously mentioned, puzzles and map exploration are great (which is why I urge to not use guides, even when you struggle). The combat is probably the weak point of the game (although this doesn't mean it's bad). Melee never ever really changes throughout the game (you only need to learn a new enemy's attack pattern every so often), and it will most likely be your main recourse as standard enemies are pretty manageable and saving ammo for tough/boss encounters is vital. Gunplay is serviceable (standard third person shooting). However enemies are pretty fun to fight, and the diversity in how they attack you helps making combat fresh for every encounter (accentuated by the level design). Boss fights are also really great (one of which is probably amongst the best in terms of "what makes a good horror game boss fight?"). While your offensive capabilities are "simple" how they are used for which enemies and which scenarios is what makes combat good.  Art direction: one of the best in horror games. The soundtrack and sound design never misses. The world and levels are scary as they are enthralling. The otherworld (and fogworld) are still one of the most unique horror aesthetics conceived. They manage to perfectly capture the feelings of "you shouldn't be here" and "this place shouldn't exist". The environments are filled with gloominess and hopelessness, with shards of hope.  The horror: excellent. The main emotion felt is "uneasy" with certain high tension scenarios. It never goes for the jumpscares, but rather heavily relies on its suspense and slow built-up for the majority of the game, which makes the tense scenarios even more impactful when they do actually happen. The first quarter of the game is mostly used to introduce its world and workings, while the last quarter is where they bump up the horror aspect.

review: The first Silent Hill I've played and I really enjoyed it. I did have to play it in shortish chunks over a few weeks because I found the atmosphere so oppressive and unsettling that I couldn't do longer sessions. I think that is a testament to how effective Bloober team was at creating an affecting experience. The audio design was a highlight for me, score and SFX included. The pulsing stingers that would play during otherwise quiet moments really instilled dread in me any time I thought I was safe. The combat SFX was especially crunchy and I really liked the sound design for all the weapons. If you like the core gameplay of RE games and don't mind something with much less levity I'd check this one out.

review: [h1]In my restless dreams, I see that town. [i]Silent Hill.[/i][/h1] [h2]Bloober Team promised they'd take me there again some day. And they did.[/h2]  I can't describe in words how happy I was when KONAMI announced the SILENT HILL 2 remake. This game holds a special place in my heart. I've played it a numerous amount of times and I was worried about the remake. Will they manage to bring the atmosphere, the aesthetics, the eeriness of the original SILENT HILL 2?   But when I started playing the game - I was surprised! They managed to capture everything and even improve upon the original. Unreal Engine 5 didn't destroy the design and art of SILENT HILL 2. The horror aspect was intact, sometimes I was spooked and even jumped out of my chair during the walkthrough.   The voice acting and scene composition are top-notch. They managed to modernize it without making it look out of place (e.g. METAL GEAR SOLID DELTA: SNAKE EATER). The character overhaul looks amazing as well, and personally, I prefer the remake versions over the originals.  But what about the sound design and music? Fear not, because Bloober Team brought the maestro Akira Yamaoka back and he (re)made the original soundtrack for the remake as well. Only the guy who created the music for the original game can outperform himself.  The only issue with this game is Unreal Engine 5, with it's constant traversal stutters, other than that, I have no complaints.  Overall, I liked the remake more than the original. Heck, I think it is better than the Resident Evil 2 remake, even though that is my personal opinion. If you are looking for an atmospheric psychological / survival horror experience, then SILENT HILL 2 is the answer for you. If you are a fan of SILENT HILL games, especially SILENT HILL 2 - IMMEDIATELY BUY IT, IT IS WORTH EVERY PENNY!  Bloober Team... You made me happy.

review: [h1]Silent Hill 2 Review[/h1]  [h2]TL;DR[/h2] This was my (Meta) first entry in the Silent Hills series, and man - what a masterpiece. It's feels like a perfect middle-ground between Resident Evil and Outlast. First playthrough was 15+ hours and it all felt amazing.  [h3]Gameplay[/h3] [list] [*][b]Combat:[/b] You're not a soldier like in RE games, and you're not a journalist like Outlast. You're a normal guy who can lay pipe.  [*][b]Replayability:[/b] Fairly high. Eight endings and NG+  [*][b]Controls:[/b] Slow, but by design. Entering rooms and rounding corners feels terrifying. [/list]  [h3]Story & World[/h3] [list] [*][b]Premise:[/b] James Sunderland arrives in Silent Hill after receiving a letter from his wife (who’s been dead for years). What follows is a descent into guilt, grief, and psychological torment.  [*][b]Characters:[/b] The characters and enemies are so well done. Every scene with Angela felt so powerful.  [*][b]Worldbuilding:[/b] Silent Hill has life(?) but feels so lonely. Atmosphere pulls you in. [/list]  [h3]Progression[/h3] [list] [*][b]100%-able?:[/b] Yes, and seems to be worth it. Each ending gives you another piece of the puzzle.  [*][b]Leveling:[/b] None, you're really just progressing through James' mind.  [*][b]Gear & Tools:[/b] Flashlight, radio, gun, pipe. Every item matters. [/list]  [h3]Presentation[/h3] [list] [*][b]Visuals:[/b] Everything feels so grotesque and unique. I imagine playing the OG was even better.  [*][b]Audio:[/b] Anxiety inducing and amazing.  [*][b]Performance:[/b] Ran fine until one cutscene, and then I dropped frames to 60fps for stream. [/list]  [h3]Bonus Bits[/h3] [list] [*][b]Mods:[/b] Not sure any are out there, or needed.  [*][b]Multiplayer:[/b] None. Silent Hill is a lonely experience.  [*][b]Steam Deck:[/b] I don't believe it's officially supported, and I don't think you'd get the same experience. [/list]

review: Silent Hill 2 - and really the entire franchise - is a unique experience in gaming. When I played the original back in my school years, I felt hopelessness, deep sorrow, and fear. For me, it was the scariest game ever – it didn’t frighten me with jump scares, but with its suffocating atmosphere. Twenty years have passed, and nothing has changed.   The remake crushes you with that same atmosphere from start to finish, carried by the legendary soundtrack of Akira Yamaoka. This is the only game where it feels literally uncomfortable to be there. You want to turn it off, to escape from it - and that is exactly where Bloober succeeded brilliantly.   Yes, there are plenty of excellent survival horrors - Alan Wake 2, Resident Evil 2, 4, 7, 8 - but only in Silent Hill 2 will you feel this. And that’s why the game remains one of a kind.   It’s also unique because of its story - so personal, so intimate for each of its characters: James, Angela, Eddie. If you love narratives rich with psychological depth, this is your game.   And for those who played the original, Bloober prepared surprises: Glimpses of the Past that reference specific moments, scenes, or items from the original game and two completely new endings. Both are worthy of the original, and one of them is so powerful it gives you chills – and you even think, “Yes, this might be the best ending for James.”   An unforgettable game. A unique survival horror. A one-of-a-kind experience that gets under your skin and never lets go.

review: 📝 English review below / Reseña en inglés más abajo  ⸻  🔶 El terror más profundo no viene de afuera, viene de adentro.  ⸻  📝 RESEÑA EN ESPAÑOL  Voy a contar un poco mi historia con este juego. La primera vez que lo jugué fue en la década de los 2000, cuando todavía no llegaba a los 15 años. No logré pasar ni un tercio porque me daba demasiado miedo, así que terminé abandonándolo.  Hoy, muchos años después, me doy cuenta de algo más fuerte: no solo no lo iba a terminar, sino que tampoco lo iba a entender. Este Silent Hill no se limita a dar miedo con monstruos o escenarios oscuros, sino que toca el verdadero terror: el que genera nuestra propia mente. Habla de traumas, de culpas, de rencores… y nos muestra que la batalla más grande es contra nosotros mismos.  Como decía Carl Jung con el concepto de la sombra, este juego nos enfrenta con esa parte oscura de nuestra psique que escondemos por miedo. En ese sentido, Silent Hill 2 Remake es tan realista como perturbador: no se trata solo de sobrevivir, sino de mirarnos en un espejo incómodo.  Lo recomiendo a quienes estén preparados para algo más que un survival horror. Porque puede ayudarnos a ser más sinceros con nosotros mismos y, en consecuencia, también con los demás.  ⸻  ✅ Puntos positivos: • Una historia profunda y psicológica. • Terror que trasciende lo superficial. • Personajes y atmósfera que dejan huella. • Excelente reinterpretación en el remake.  ❌ Puntos negativos: • No es para cualquiera: puede ser demasiado perturbador. • Jugabilidad que en algunos momentos se siente pesada. • Exige estar en el “estado mental” correcto para apreciarlo.  ⸻  🎯 Conclusión:  Más que un juego de terror, es un viaje a lo más oscuro de la mente humana. Silent Hill 2 Remake no solo asusta: confronta, incomoda y deja pensando. Una experiencia única para quienes se animen a mirarse dentro.  🔸 PUNTUACIÓN FINAL: 9/10 El miedo más real es el que llevamos dentro.  ⸻  📝 REVIEW IN ENGLISH  🔶 The deepest fear doesn’t come from the outside — it comes from within.  ⸻  Let me share a bit of my story with this game. The first time I played it was back in the 2000s, when I was under 15 years old. I couldn’t get past even a third of the game because it scared me so much, so I abandoned it.  Today, looking back as an adult, I realize something bigger: not only was I not going to finish it, I wasn’t even going to understand it. This Silent Hill doesn’t just scare with monsters or dark environments — it dives into the fear created by our own minds. It’s about trauma, guilt, resentment… and it shows us that the greatest battle is against ourselves.  As Carl Jung described with the concept of the shadow, this game confronts us with the darkest part of our psyche that we hide out of fear. In that sense, Silent Hill 2 Remake is as realistic as it is disturbing: it’s not just about surviving, it’s about facing an uncomfortable reflection.  I recommend it to those who are ready for something deeper than a survival horror. It can genuinely help us treat ourselves — and others — more sincerely.  ⸻  ✅ Pros: • Deep, psychological storytelling. • Fear that goes beyond the superficial. • Memorable characters and atmosphere. • Strong reinterpretation in the remake.  ❌ Cons: • Not for everyone: can be too disturbing. • Gameplay can feel heavy at times. • Requires the right mental state to fully appreciate.  ⸻  🎯 Conclusion:  More than a horror game, it’s a journey into the darkest corners of the human mind. Silent Hill 2 Remake doesn’t just scare — it confronts, unsettles, and lingers. A unique experience for those brave enough to look within.  🔸 FINAL SCORE: 9/10 The scariest fear is the one we carry inside.
